newsitem.title: USA: Plaintiffs hail verdict against O.J. Simpson.
newsitem.headline: Plaintiffs hail verdict against O.J. Simpson.

text.p: With O.J. Simpson's defence team considering an appeal, the plaintiffs' attorneys on Tuesday defended the jury verdicts finding the ex-football star responsible for two killings and ordering him to pay $33.5 million in damages.
"The jury acted within its discretion. This man committed a double murder and it found it was not appropriate for him to profit from these murders," said attorney Daniel Petrocelli.

The lawyer, who represents the father of murder victim Ronald Goldman, said he did not believe Monday's award of $25 million in punitive damages on top of $8.5 million in compensatory damages was excessive.

"If Mr. (Fred) Goldman had his way, this man would never walk the streets (again)," he said on NBC's "Today" programme. "The money represents punishment and it's the only punishment allowed under the law."

Denise Brown, a sister of Simpson's slain ex-wife Nicole Brown Simpson, said the damage award was entirely appropriate. "This is hell on Earth for him (Simpson), because the most important thing for him is money.
"He said he would kill her and get away with it, and you know what? He didn't," Brown told the "Today" show.
For their part Simpson's defence team maintained a virtual public silence after winning a 10-day delay before plaintiffs can go after Simpson's assets.

However, attorney Robert Blasier, a member of the defence team, appeared on the "Today" show to say Simpson was "very disappointed. The amount is very high and we expect it to be reduced within the scope of other cases."
Blasier said estimates by plaintiffs' experts that Simpson could make $2 million to $3 million from autographed sports memorabilia were "not the case now.
"We are just sitting back to see what will happen," he said when asked what the defence's next move would be.

Simpson, a football star who became a bit-part actor and television personality, was acquitted by a predominantly black criminal court jury in 1995 of murdering Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman.
But the families of the victims sued in civil court for damages and the mostly white jury in Santa Monica unanimously found him responsible for the deaths.

Legal observers said the defence might file an appeal -- although that would require posting a bond of 1-1/2 times the amount of compensatory damages. They may also ask Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki to reduce the award, arguing it was excessive.

Simpson was reportedly at a golf course when Monday's verdict was read and then drove to the office of lead defence attorney Robert Baker, along with his business attorney Skip Taft, apparently to discuss the next move.
Harvard University law professor Alan Dershowitz, who was an adviser to Simpson's criminal defence team in 1995, said there were several grounds for an appeal.
One area of contention, he said, was whether blacks were unfairly excluded from the jury selection process.

Dershowitz also said there might be grounds for appeal on the fact that the civil trial jury was allowed to hear that Simpson had failed a lie-detector test -- when such polygraphs are usually not allowed in evidence in California courts.

Also the defence could argue that Fujisaki should not have allowed the jury to hear testimony from a woman at a shelter for abused women who said she took a call from a woman named "Nicole" who said her high-profile ex-husband had stalked and threatened her. The call came a few days before the June 12, 1994, murders.
Leo Terrell, a civil rights lawyer and sometime Simpson family spokesman, declared the punitive award "illegal," adding: "I guarantee there's going to be an appeal."

On Tuesday Terrell, who is black, said "unfortunately, this case had racial overtones." He pointed to the fact that a black woman alternate juror said she felt Simpson should not have been found responsible for the deaths and that she believed the police planted some evidence to frame him.

Edward Medvene, one of the plaintiffs' attorneys shot back that the verdict would have been the same regardless of the racial makeup of the jury. "This was a race-blind case about Mr. Simpson's liability," he said on the "Today" show.
In the final phase of the civil trial, Baker argued Simpson was virtually broke even though he lives in a mansion, drives a Bentley and employs his own bodyguard.
The plaintiffs, however, presented witnesses who said Simpson was worth $15.7 million and could earn between $2 million and $3 million a year by cashing in on his notoriety.
